title: Email Writing — subject line, tone, format
notes: **What it is:** a letter sent digitally — block format plus To/Subject fields. The examiner mainly checks the SUBJECT line and whether tone matches the receiver.

**Structure:** To → Subject (short phrase, not a sentence) → Salutation matched to receiver ('Dear Principal,' vs 'Hi Anisha,') → 1–2 short paragraphs (purpose → details → courteous close) → Sign-off (formal: Yours faithfully + full name; informal: Best wishes + first name).
**Register decides grammar:** the same message shifts — 'could you please' vs 'can you', 'I require' vs 'I need'. Present perfect introduces news ('I have prepared…').
**Never write a lazy subject** ('Queries') — a precise subject is itself worth marks.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

**Complete email format — formal:**
To: [recipient@email.com]
Subject: [Specific, informative subject line — 5-10 words]

Dear [Title + Last Name],

[Opening sentence stating purpose]

[Body: 2-3 paragraphs with details, facts, context]

[Closing: polite request, next steps, or gratitude]

Yours faithfully,
[Full Name]
[Contact number / ID if relevant]

**Complete email format — informal:**
To: [friend@email.com]
Subject: [Casual but clear subject]

Hi/Say hello to [Name],

[Warm opening — react to last message / ask about them]

[Body: 1-2 paragraphs, natural tone, contractions OK]

[Closing: anticipation of reply / warm wish]

Best wishes / Love / Talk soon,
[First Name]

**Subject line — the first impression:** A good subject line is: SPECIFIC (not 'Help'), INFORMATIVE (not 'Urgent' — that's manipulative), and SCANNABLE (under 60 characters so it doesn't truncate). Good: 'Request for Library Committee Membership — Class 11'. Bad: 'I want to join library'. The subject line must reflect the email's content accurately. A mismatched subject is a major deduction.

**Subject line patterns by email type:** (1) *Request*: 'Request for Academic Leave — [Date]' (2) *Application*: 'Application for Student Council Position — [Name]' (3) *Complaint*: 'Complaint: Defective Product Order #[Number]' (4) *Inquiry*: 'Inquiry: Tuition Fee Structure for 2025-26' (5) *Thank you*: 'Thank You — [Event Name]' (6) *Follow-up*: 'Follow-up: Previous Discussion on [Topic]' (7) *Informal*: 'Re: Trip Plan' or 'Checking In!'

**Tone matching — the #1 examiner criterion:** Formal email to a teacher/official: 'Dear Dr. Sharma,' + 'I am writing to request…' + 'I would be grateful…' + 'Yours faithfully'. Informal email to a friend: 'Hey Priya!' + 'Just wanted to check…' + 'See you soon!' + 'Talk later'. Writing a formal email to a friend with stiff language or an informal email to a principal with slang both lose marks. Match the tone to the recipient.

**Present perfect for email news:** English emails uniquely favour present perfect ('I have attached…', 'I have prepared…', 'I have completed…') to introduce news or updates. Simple past ('I attached…') sounds like the attachment is in the past. Use present perfect when something relevant to NOW is being mentioned. 'I have written the essay you requested' → still relevant because they might want to see it now.

**Email body structure — short paragraphs:** Unlike letters, emails use shorter paragraphs (2-4 sentences). Email is inherently quick-read. Use subheadings or bullet points for multiple questions or items. 'Could you please clarify: (1) deadline, (2) fee structure, (3) application process?' This makes your email scannable and professional.

**Call to action — what you want from the recipient:** Every functional email must end with a clear action: 'Please confirm your availability by Friday.' 'Kindly review and provide feedback at your earliest convenience.' 'I look forward to your response.' Vague closings ('Let me know' without saying what) lose marks. Make your ask specific and time-bound if possible.

**Common email mistakes in exams:** (1) Subject line missing or vague — automatic deduction. (2) Wrong salutation/register — 'Hey Sir!' or 'Dear buddy'. (3) No clear purpose in opening — rambling to get there. (4) Overly casual tone in formal emails — slang, emojis, abbreviations. (5) Overly formal tone in informal emails — 'I am writing to inform you that…' to a friend. (6) No sign-off or wrong sign-off. (7) Forgetting to mention attachments. (8) Writing more than 150 words for a formal email or 120 for informal.

**Cc, Bcc, and Reply All — real vs. exam awareness:** In exams, you write the email body only — no need to write To/Cc/Bcc fields unless asked. But know the difference: Cc = visible to all, copies (people who should know but don't need to act). Bcc = invisible copies (privacy). Reply All = responds to everyone in To and Cc. 'Reply All' in real life is often frowned upon.

**Email vs. Formal Letter — what changes:** Keep: formal tone, structure, politeness, no contractions (formal). Drop: address blocks at top and bottom, date on a separate line, 'Enclosure' (use 'Attachment' instead). Add: 'To:' and 'Subject:' fields. Shorter paragraphs, bullet points OK. Email is the modern shorthand of the formal letter.

**Replying to emails — proper etiquette:** When replying, keep the original subject line (add 'Re:' automatically in most systems). Don't start a new thread unless the topic changed completely. Reference the specific point you're answering. Keep replies concise — don't re-quoting the entire original email. Use 'As you mentioned…' or 'Regarding your question about…' to show you read it.

**Professional email vocabulary for exams:** 'I am writing to enquire about…' 'Could you please provide…' 'I would appreciate your guidance on…' 'Please find attached…' 'Kindly acknowledge receipt of this email.' 'I look forward to hearing from you.' 'Thank you for your time and consideration.' Master these phrases — they work in any formal email scenario.
confusion: Email subject line vs. Letter subject line: Both should be specific, but email subjects are typically SHORTER (3-8 words vs 5-10 words for letters). Email subjects can be slightly more casual. Letter subjects often include reference numbers or file numbers. Email subjects never include 'Ref:' — letters do.

Yours faithfully in email vs. letter: The rule is the same — 'Dear Sir/Madam' = 'Yours faithfully'; 'Dear Mr. Sharma' = 'Yours sincerely'. But in email, this pairing is often ignored by learners, leading to register confusion. In exams, the pairing rule still applies even if emails are informal in practice.

Attachment vs. Enclosure in email: Never use 'Enclosure' in an email — the correct term is 'Attachment' or 'I have attached…'. 'Enclosure' is for physical documents inside a physical envelope. Using 'Enclosure' in an email signals that the student doesn't understand the medium.

Informal email vs. informal letter: Informal emails to friends are almost identical in tone to informal letters. The main differences are structural: email has To/Subject fields, is typically shorter, and can use bullet points. Letters have addresses and date blocks. In exams, the format differences determine the marks.

Reply vs. Forward: A REPLY goes back to the original sender. A FORWARD sends the email to someone else, often with your added comments. In exams, never confuse these — if asked to 'reply', send back to the original. If asked to 'forward', send to a third party.
practice: Write a formal email (120-150 words) to the Principal requesting permission to organise a 'Clean Campus' awareness campaign. Include: purpose, proposed date, budget (approximate), and a specific request for approval. Use a precise subject line and formal tone throughout.

Write an informal email (100-120 words) to your best friend telling them about your exciting trip to Chitwan National Park. Use: contractions, question tags, natural tone, and a warm closing. Include a subject line that matches the tone.

Write a formal email (100-120 words) to the Manager of a bookshop enquiring about a bulk discount on NCERT textbooks for your school library. Ask 3 specific questions (price per copy, minimum quantity, delivery time).
Convert this informal sentence to formal email register: 'Hey, just wanted to check if you got my last email. Can you reply soon? Thx!' Then explain what three changes you made and why each matters.

Write a formal email (100 words) to your class teacher reporting that the project work submitted by your group was accidentally deleted. Apologise, explain briefly, and request an extension. Use a clear subject line and professional tone.
universalFacts: The first email was sent in 1971 by Ray Tomlinson, who chose the '@' symbol to separate the user from the machine. The original test message was 'QWERTYUIOP' — the computer doesn't remember the meaning, but the format was revolutionary.

In the NEB English exam, email writing typically carries 5-8 marks. The subject line alone is often worth 1 mark. A vague or missing subject line is one of the most common errors students make, and examiners explicitly note it in mark schemes.

Research on email readability shows that people scan emails in an 'F-pattern': left edge first, then top horizontal scan, then partial vertical scan. This means the subject line and first 2-3 lines of your email body get the most attention.

The formal email as a genre is still relatively young (only ~30 years), but it has already developed strict conventions: subject line, salutation, clear opening, structured body, call to action, formal sign-off. These conventions mirror formal letters but are compressed for speed.

Studies show that email communication creates a 'context collapse' — the same message is read by colleagues, managers, and sometimes family. This is why email tone matters more than social media tone. In exams, matching tone to recipient is the #1 criterion tested.
